k-1.x_notes: Six problems on 8 pages, all boards at actual size with block icons for non-readers. P1 (4 shapes) includes a 12-triangle trapezoid with 7 up and 5 down triangles, an even-area board that cannot be covered, which is a good K-level surprise. P2 asks for fewest greens on triangles of side 2, 3 and 4 (answers 2, 3, 4). P4 asks for fewest blocks with yellow/red/blue/green; the answers (3, 6, 5) are not obvious, since three trapezoids beat the hexagon solution. P5 asks the children to build each 2x shape from its own small blocks. Green and red can be built; the 2x hexagon (at most 3 hexagons fit) and the 2x chevron cannot. This is a rich, very concrete investigation. P6 is a game with tally boxes. Its three boards give little contrast: the hexagon is a second-player win, and the strips of 8 and 10 are both first-player wins by the same symmetry. Defect: P3 says to cover each copy 'in a different way', but each family has one more copy than there are tilings (3 hexagons for 2 ways, 4 for 3, 5 for 4), so the stated task is impossible. Rewording to 'find all the ways' is a quick fix. A 'How many?' box beside impossible shapes is slightly confusing.
k-1.y_notes: Six problems on 6 pages, all at actual size. P1 has six shapes with a good spread: an odd trapezoid, the 8-triangle cut-off triangle (even area but 5 up / 3 down), and a chevron that works. It asks the children to mark the impossible ones and say why, which is good K-1 reasoning. P2 is the same as X. P3 is worded correctly ('Find all the ways') over 2 and 3 tilings. P4 asks for fewest blocks with the chevron included (answers 3, 3, 4). Both the parallelogram and the trapezoid reward going beyond the obvious covering. P5 is a game with five short boards whose answers vary (strips of 4, 5, 6, 7 give F, S, F, F, and the hexagon gives S), so it gives better data for finding a pattern than X's game. P6 asks for all 6 tilings of the (1,2,2) hexagon drawn on half-size copies. This is a real bridge to kernel 2, but too hard for kindergartners to draw. It has nothing like X's rep-tile exploration, and it is slightly shorter overall.
k-1.reason: Both are solid and correct apart from X's P3 wording. X's rep-tile problem and fewest-blocks page give K-1 more substantial, concrete work. The P3 wording takes seconds to fix, while Y's last problem is a stretch for kindergartners.

grades-2-3.x_notes: Seven well-sequenced problems with large, actual-size boards and recording boxes. P1: A yes, B no (odd), C no (side-4 triangle, even area, 10 up / 6 down), D yes. P2: fewest greens on triangles of side 3, 4, 5. P3: four side-2 hexagons each missing two triangles, a direct analogue of the mutilated checkerboard (a and c can be covered, b and d cannot), with lines for explanations. P4: a side-7 triangle needing 7 greens, with an explanation; this mostly repeats P2 at larger size. P5: chevrons against blues on sides 3, 4, 6 (5/3, 4/4, 8/6) and why chevrons can never do better. The prompt is wordy and multi-part. P6: two boards with equal up and down counts that still need 2 and 4 greens because of a bottleneck. This is a real deepening of kernel 1, though hard to explain at this age. P7: draw a connected board needing at least 3 greens with as few triangles as possible (answer 7), a good open design problem. All answers check. The packet runs to 11 pages and is a bit text-heavy in places.
grades-2-3.y_notes: Seven concise problems. P1: a star whose tiling is forced (yes), an odd triangle (no), the 12-triangle trapezoid (no, 7 up / 5 down) and a (2,1,1) hexagon (yes). P2: hexagons with holes. E is unbalanced (no), G is balanced and tileable, and F is a bowtie meeting at a single point, balanced overall but impossible. P3: fewest greens on sides 2 to 5, then explain the biggest. P4 generalizes to sides 10 and 100 without building, a good step toward a rule. P5 reuses the P3 triangles for chevrons with a comparison table (2 to 5) and asks whether chevrons can ever beat blues. P6: design a 20-triangle board needing at least 6 greens (feasible, open, hard). P7: place two greens anywhere on a side-2 hexagon and find and justify the rule. I checked all 144 up/down pairs and every one can be covered, so 'one up, one down' is exactly right. This is a strong open investigation. All mathematics checks. It uses less text than X, with somewhat fewer boards.
grades-2-3.reason: Both develop kernel 1 thoroughly and correctly. X's strengths are more boards and the bottleneck boards; Y's are less reading, the 10/100 generalization and an excellent rule-finding investigation. I would be equally happy with either.

grades-4-5.x_notes: This is an excellent, coherent development of kernel 2. P1 asks for all tilings of hexagons (1,1,1), (1,1,2), (1,2,2), giving 2, 3, 6, with half-size drawing copies. P2 builds the flip graph on C (the greatest distance is 4). P3 introduces a chain of flat rhombi from the bottom edge, shown in a correct worked picture (RLRR). It asks whether the chain determines the tiling and what a flip does to it (it swaps an adjacent pair). P4 counts the (1,2,3), (1,3,3) and (1,4,4) hexagons, giving 10, 20 and 70, so the chain becomes a counting tool. P5 has three flip puzzles with the start covering printed at actual size to build on and a small finish picture. I verified the minimum flips as 2, 6 and 8; the c pair is the maximum distance, and the children must justify it. P6 asks for round trips of 4 and 6 flips and why odd round trips are impossible. P7 counts the 20 tilings of the side-2 hexagon. Weaknesses: P3 and P5 are long; P2 reveals that hexagon C has six ways before P1's 'explain how you know' is settled; the packet is 11 pages.
grades-4-5.y_notes: The content is very similar and correct. P1 asks for the 6 tilings of the (1,2,2) hexagon, with 10 small boards. P2 is the flip graph, but the children must redraw all their P1 coverings on new boards, which is busywork. P3 has three flip puzzles copied from small pictures onto one blank actual-size board. I verified the minimums as 3, 4 and 8, and E to F is the maximum. P4 asks for a 4-flip round trip and whether 5 or 7 flips are possible. P5 defines ribbons with a correct example (LRRLR) and asks what a flip does to the two ribbons of the side-2 hexagon. That is deeper than X's single chain. P6 is a page of lines for the parity and E-to-F explanations, which partly repeats P4. P7 asks for all 20 tilings of the side-2 hexagon to be drawn on 25 small hexagons, which is a lot of drawing. P8 counts the (1,3,3) hexagon (20) by ribbons. The text is more concise, but there are fewer counting steps before the general count, and more drawing overhead.
grades-4-5.reason: Both are mathematically sound. X's sequence of counts (2, 3, 6, then 10, 20, 70) uses the chain idea better, and its flip puzzles start from coverings printed at actual size. Y adds redraw busywork and copying covering A from a small picture.

overall.reason: The packets are close in quality, and every problem checks except X's mis-worded K-1 P3, which takes moments to fix. X gives K-1 a richer concrete investigation (the rep-tiles) and gives 4-5 a better-developed and more practical route from tilings through chains to counting. Grades 2-3 is a toss-up, so X gets a slight edge overall.
